entries.x: One business process per journey. Each lane is a role on the personas page; each task names the skill that performs it. The BPMN source of each process is in processes/content/ , copied into the guide as input/business-processes/ . Select a diagram to open it in the process viewer, which lists each task and the skill that performs it. Process Lanes BPMN --- --- --- J1 Issue the newborn's birth-dose DVCs in Country A Caregiver, Birth clinic vaccinator, Birth clinic issuing system, Issuer signing key j1-birth-dose-dvc.bpmn J2 Discover and refer an unregistered infant in Country B Caregiver, Community health worker, CHW app j2-chw-discovery-referral.bpmn J3 Verify, import and schedule at the home clinic Caregiver, Home clinic provider, Home clinic EHR j3-clinic-verification-schedule.bpmn J4.0 Issue the family's records to one phone as VHLs Caregiver, National health portal, Issuer signing key, Family phone j4-0-family-vhl-issuance.bpmn J4.1 Read a family member's records at the point of care abroad Caregiver, Family phone, Point-of-care provider, Point-of-care receiver j4-1-vhl-point-of-care.bpmn J1 Issue the newborn's birth-dose DVCs in Country A Process id Process J1BirthDoseDvc . Open in the process viewer. J1, Cross-border birth and initial vaccination. In Country A (XXR, the birth country) the provincial hospital gives Chanthala's Hep B and BCG birth doses and issues one signed DVC per dose (DVCMinPreQual at subclaim -6) as a paper QR: the guide's QR Code Generation section 12 example. The hospital system is the Issuer (SMART Trust) and the HCERT side of the VHL Sharer; the private key stays with the key holder (two-phase signing, STT-ISS-004, STT-COS-006). XXR's DSC, under its CSCA, being on the GDHCN trust list is a PRECONDITION of issuing, declared below, not a step. Mali is the Holder (SMART Trust, smart-trust-phw) and VHL Holder (IHE ITI VHL). Task checklist: j1-birth-dose-dvc.checklist.md. J2 Discover and refer an unregistered infant in Country B Process id Process J2ChwDiscovery . Open in the process viewer. J2, Return home, CHW discovery and referral. Back in Country B (home, XXH), where the family resides, the community health worker finds Chanthala unregistered on a home visit. Offline, the CHW app reads the foreign DVCs without verifying them (read-unverified, STT-VER-011: the triage read stops before the trust lookup and marks every field unverified), registers the infant and refers her to the clinic for verification. The CHW app is a Receiver (SMART Trust, smart-trust-phw) that deliberately stops before trust; Mali provides the VDHC as Holder (smart-trust-phw requirement provide-a-vhl-to-a-receiver). Task checklist: j2-chw-discovery-referral.checklist.md. J3 Verify, import and schedule at the home clinic Process id Process J3ClinicVerification . Open in the process viewer. J3, Clinic verification and schedule generation, in Country B. The clinic EHR (Receiver in SMART Trust and smart-trust-phw, VHL Receiver side in IHE ITI VHL) holds a copy of the GDHCN trust list, which the trust anchor (Trust Network Anchor; IHE Trust Anchor) distributes and Country B, a Trust Network Participant, retrieves (smart-trust-phw retrieve-pki-material). Loading the DID documents is a PRECONDITION of this visit, not a step in it: the clinic may be offline throughout, so the list it verifies against is the one it last refreshed, about weekly, when the CHW visits the base clinic or district health office. It verifies each foreign DVC in the STT-VER-001 order against XXR's DSC DID document, imports the verified doses and evaluates the national schedule, which finds birth-dose OPV due. Task checklist: j3-clinic-verification-schedule.checklist.md. J4.0 Issue the family's records to one phone as VHLs Process id Process J40FamilyVhl . Open in the process viewer. J4.0, Outbound family travel, "One Family, One Phone". Before travelling, Mali asks Country B's national portal for each family member's records. The portal, a VHL Sharer (IHE ITI VHL) and Issuer (SMART Trust, smart-trust-phw), issues one passcode-protected Verifiable Health Link per member: the documents (IPS, DVCs) encrypted as JWE (STT-VHL-007) behind an ITI-YY5 manifest, the link in the SMART Health Links payload format at HCERT key 5 (STT-VHL-001, STT-VHL-002), signed with Country B's DSC. The shared phone holds the QRs for Mali, the VHL Holder. Task checklist: j4-0-family-vhl-issuance.checklist.md. J4.1 Read a family member's records at the point of care abroad Process id Process J41VhlFetch . Open in the process viewer. J4.1. Abroad, Chanthala needs care. Mali, the VHL Holder (IHE ITI VHL; Holder in SMART Trust and smart-trust-phw, requirement provide-a-vhl-to-a-receiver), opens her QR on the family phone and tells the passcode. The hospital system, a VHL Receiver (Receiver in SMART Trust and smart-trust-phw), verifies the HCERT against the GDHCN trust list, requests the manifest by ITI-YY5 with an HTTP Message Signature (STT-VHL-005, STT-VHL-006, STT-VHL-008) and decrypts the documents (STT-VHL-007). If the HCERT does not verify, there is no digital verification: the VHL is not followed and the records are treated like paper. As in J3, loading the DID documents is a PRECONDITION of this visit, not a step in it: the hospital verifies against its cached copy of the trust list and needs no connection to do so. It refreshes that cache nightly or hourly, where an offline site such as the J3 clinic refreshes about weekly. Task checklist: j4-1-vhl-point-of-care.checklist.md.

The journeys do not restate requirements. Each step of a user scenario names the requirement it exercises by its id (for example STT-VER-011, read without verifying, in J2). Those requirements are defined, with their tests, on smart-trust-tools' requirements page (sources in skills/requirements), which traces them to WHO SMART Trust and IHE ITI VHL. The WHO SMART Trust PHW requirements map onto the journeys as follows: provide-a-vhl-to-a-receiver (Holder): J2, J3 and J4.1. receive-a-vhl (Receiver): J2, J3 and J4.1. publish- , receive- , distribute- and retrieve-pki-material : the trust anchor and the participants, preconditions of J1, J3, J4.0 and J4.1.

This guide is the WHO SMART Guidelines L2 digital adaptation kit (DAK) and L3 implementation guide of the SMART Trust demonstrator. It follows one family across borders through four journeys: Journey Where --- --- --- J1 Issue the newborn's birth-dose DVCs Country A (XXR) J2 Discover and refer an unregistered infant Country B (home) J3 Verify, import and schedule at the home clinic Country B (home) J4.0 Issue the family's records to one phone as VHLs Country B (home) J4.1 Read a family member's records at the point of care abroad abroad The journeys exercise the HCERT and VHL libraries of smart-trust-tools against WHO SMART Trust and WHO SMART Trust PHW. Every person in them is fictional. Generic personas and system actors: the roles that play each process lane. User scenarios: the user stories and the journeys step by step. Business processes: one BPMN process per journey. Functional requirements: where the journeys' requirements are defined. The project: the journeys J1 to J4 in full, the plan, the app-platform proposal and the dependency register. The source is litlfred/smart-trust-demo. This guide is a demonstrator, not WHO guidance.

User scenarios Each step names the requirements of smart-trust-tools it exercises. The stories are in scenarios/stories.json . J1 — Cross-border birth and initial vaccination (Country A) Precondition: the issuer's DSC is on the trust list. XXR's document signer certificate (DSC), issued under XXR's Country Signing CA (CSCA), was shared with the GDHCN, the Trust Anchor, before any DVC is signed; the GDHCN publishes it as a DID document. Sharing it is not a step of issuing. A DVC signed with a key whose DSC was never shared fails every receiver's trust-list check (STT-VER-006). Mali gives birth to Chanthala on 2026-10-21 at a provincial hospital in Country A, while visiting relatives. Dr Pimchanok WATTANA gives the Hep B and BCG birth doses and records them. For each dose, the hospital system does three things: 1. It builds a DVCMinPreQual payload: STT-PAY-001…005 and STT-PAY-007, with subclaim −6 (STT-SEL-003). 2. It prepares the CWT and the bytes to sign: STT-CWT-001…005, STT-ISS-004. 3. It has XXR's key sign them (STT-COS-002, STT-COS-006), then finishes the HC1 text: STT-COS-001, STT-ZIP-001, STT-B45-001, STT-HC1-001, STT-QR-001. Mali leaves with two paper DVCs. In the demo: the guide's two signed HC1 strings stand in for the hospital's output. Live issuance in the app uses a TEST-ONLY key (STT-ISS-003), whose DSC is not on the GDHCN list, so its DVCs do not verify in J3. J2 — Return home, CHW discovery and referral (Country B) Back in Country B, Sita RAI finds Chanthala missing from the household register on a home visit. Sita has no signal. She scans both QRs. The CHW app reads them with read-unverified (STT-VER-011; STT-B45-002, STT-ZIP-002, STT-CBR-003), which needs no trust list. It shows the doses, marked unverified. Sita registers Chanthala and refers her to the clinic. Everything syncs that evening. J3 — Clinic verification and schedule generation (Country B) Precondition: the DID documents are already loaded. Loading them is not a step of this visit. The clinic may be offline all day, so the EHR fetches nothing during it: its trust store holds the GDHCN DEV trust list as it was last refreshed, including XXR's DSC DID document (STT-TRU-001, STT-TRU-002, STT-TRU-005). A clinic with no connection of its own refreshes it about weekly, when the CHW visits the base clinic or district health office, where Country B retrieves the list the GDHCN trust anchor distributes. A DSC published after that refresh is not in the clinic's copy, so its DVC fails the trust-list check (STT-VER-006) until the next refresh. Tomas ALVES opens the referral and scans the QRs. The EHR verifies each DVC offline against that copy (STT-VER-001…009, STT-KID-002). Both verify, so it imports them as FHIR Immunization s with provenance (STT-VER-007, STT-VER-008). The national schedule then runs: the birth doses count, and birth-dose OPV is due. Tomas gives it. If a DVC fails, the EHR names the step and the reason, and Tomas decides by national policy. J4.0 — "One Family, One Phone" (Country B) Precondition, as in J1: Country B's DSC, under Country B's CSCA, is already shared with the GDHCN, the Trust Anchor. That is what lets the hospital abroad verify the link in J4.1. The family plans a trip. On the national portal, Mali asks for each member's records. For each member, the portal does three things: 1. It assembles an IPS and that member's DVCs. 2. It encrypts them (STT-VHL-004, STT-VHL-007) behind a passcode-protected manifest with an expiry (STT-VHL-009). 3. It issues the link as an HCERT, with the VHL at key 5 (STT-VHL-001, STT-VHL-002), signed with Country B's DSC. The shared phone holds one QR per member. J4.1 — Point of care abroad Precondition, as in J3: the DID documents are already loaded. The hospital system's trust store is a cached copy of the GDHCN trust list, including Country B's DSC DID document (STT-TRU-001, STT-TRU-002, STT-TRU-005). The hospital refreshes it nightly or hourly, against about weekly at the offline J3 clinic. It does not need to be online to verify: verifying reads the cache and never fetches the list. A DSC published after the last refresh fails the trust-list check (STT-VER-006), naming that reason. Abroad, Chanthala has a fever. Mali shows Chanthala's QR on the family phone and tells Dr Ana MOREIRA the passcode. The hospital system takes four steps: 1. It verifies the HCERT against Country B's DSC in that copy of the trust list. 2. It requests the manifest by ITI-YY5, signed with HTTP Message Signatures (STT-VHL-005, STT-VHL-006, STT-VHL-008). 3. It decrypts the IPS and DVCs (STT-VHL-007). 4. It shows them to Dr Ana MOREIRA. If the HCERT does not verify (for example, Country B's DSC is missing from the cached list), there is no digital verification. The hospital names the step and the reason (STT-VER-008), does not follow the VHL, and Dr Ana MOREIRA treats whatever the family can show as she would a paper record.

Google Maven artifacts (AGP, AndroidX test) are pinned with sha256 like every other. The emulator job uses a pinned action by SHA and caches no unverified artifacts. 5. The app (Started: app/ , J2's offline read, and J3's verification and import of the guide's DVCs on Android, workflow app.yml . A verified DVC becomes a FHIR R4 Immunization with its Provenance ( dev.ohs.fhir:fhir-model-r4 ); an unverified one is not imported. Next: J3's schedule, then J1 issuance.) On the base the owner chooses from the proposal (recommended: a lean Compose Multiplatform app on the OHS KMP libraries, Android first): J1: clinic issues the newborn's DVC (bundled test key standing in for the clinic's DSC, or the Keystore), prints/shows the QR. J2: CHW scans the paper QR offline ( readUnverified ), registers the infant (SDC questionnaire), creates a referral ( ServiceRequest ). J3: clinic verifies against the bundled DEV trust list, imports the Immunization s into the on-device FHIR engine, evaluates the schedule ( PlanDefinition/$apply ), shows the next doses. J4: portal issues per-member VHL QRs to the shared phone; a receiver fetches the manifest (ITI-YY5) from a local test sharer and decrypts. An emulator UI test drives the four journeys end to end. 6. Web and publication The web target (once hcert-core runs in a browser, or via the Rust/wasm library meanwhile), and the gh-pages site (agent-published): the journeys, BPMN viewers, personas and the test evidence. Open items Network: this session cannot reach dl.google.com (Google Maven, the Android SDK). Steps 4–5 need it locally to write the verification metadata; the owner can allow it in the environment's network settings. Browser build of hcert-core (for the web target): to be raised in smart-trust-tools. Android algorithm names: hcert-core's JVM code asks for RSASSA-PSS , which Android's providers may not offer under that name; step 4 will show.

Status: decided 2026-10-23: option B, staged, with the Rust/wasm library for the web meanwhile (memory/dir-app-platform.md). Researched 2026-10-23. Question: on what should the J1–J4 app be built, so that it runs the Kotlin HCERT library on Android (and, ideally, the web) on the most recent, most Kotlin-native Open Health Stack? 1. What Open Health Stack is today Open Health Stack (OHS) began as a Google-led set of components and is now the OHS Software Foundation , a community project under the Linux Foundation, which WHO joined in July 2026. Its code lives in github.com/ohs-foundation (28 repositories). There are two generations of the client libraries: Generation Libraries Platforms Distribution State --- --- --- --- --- android-fhir (first) com.google.android.fhir:engine , data-capture (SDC), workflow , knowledge Android only Google Maven "Maintenance"; last commit Feb–Mar 2026. Workflow runs CQL (HAPI-based, heavy). Kotlin Multiplatform (current) dev.ohs.fhir:fhir-model-r4 1.0.0-rc03, fhir-path-r4 , fhir-engine 2.0.0-alpha04, fhir-data-capture 2.0.0-alpha04, fhir-workflow 2.0.0-alpha01; dev.ohs.player:client 1.0.0-alpha03 Android, desktop JVM, iOS, web (wasmJs, and JS for some) Maven Central Active (commits this week); alpha APIs. Workflow does PlanDefinition/$apply ; CQL is "still to come". On top of the KMP generation sits the OHS Player , described by the foundation as a cross-stack reference toolkit, "reference, not product": player-reference : the client, a GitHub template app in Compose Multiplatform (Android, iOS, desktop, web from one tree). Screens are driven by configuration (SQL-on-FHIR ViewDefinition s compiled at build time), data entry by SDC questionnaires. It opens on an OIDC login and blocks on a first sync with a FHIR server; there is no bundled-data mode. player-client : the library behind it (configuration-driven FHIR views), usable on its own. ohs-player-reference-web-portal : a TypeScript admin portal for workforce hierarchies (users, access). Not a clinical web app; not relevant to J1–J4. ohs-player-reference-backend , -infrastructure : backend and deployment (FHIR gateway, data pipes). player-reference-examples : variants of the reference app (empty today). A natural place to offer the journeys upstream later — an OHS Foundation repository, so only by proposal, never from here. The most recent and most Kotlin-native choice is therefore the KMP generation , with or without the Player template. 2. Constraints every option must meet 1. The Android emulator test of the HCERT library (STT-GEN-004) must run in CI on an Android runtime, platform crypto included. This is independent of the app: it is a small Android test module that depends only on the HCERT jar (plan step 4). It can land before the app decision. 2. Offline and serverless demo. J2 is offline by definition, and CI cannot stand up an OIDC provider and FHIR server for an emulator run cheaply. The app needs a bundled-data mode. 3. Supply chain. Every artifact pinned with sha256, releases ≥ 14 days old, no install scripts. Fewer dependencies is better. 4. The HCERT library comes from a pinned smart-trust-tools commit as a JVM jar (owner's choice). On Android the JVM jar works as is. On the web it does not yet: hcert-core's Kotlin/JS target uses node:crypto and node:zlib , so it runs on Node, not in a browser, and there is no wasmJs target. Any web front end needs either a browser target in hcert-core (WebCrypto, CompressionStream ), a library change in smart-trust-tools, or the Rust/wasm library, which already runs in the browser with WebCrypto keys. 3. Options Option A — Fork the OHS Player reference app Create the app from the player-reference template; add an offline demo mode (bundled FHIR bundle, no login), the J1–J4 screens and the HCERT calls. Pros Cons --- --- It is the OHS Player: the most visibly "OHS" outcome, and the closest to what OHS implementers will start from. Requires an OIDC provider and a FHIR server to start; the offline mode is ours to write and to keep merging against a template that moves weekly. Android, iOS, desktop and web from one tree; configuration-driven screens; SDC questionnaires for registration (J2) and import (J3) come wired. 57 libraries and 8 plugins in its catalogue (Koin, Ktor CIO/Darwin, Kermit, ksafe, kotlinpoet, BigNum, Compose adaptive …), several alpha, plus their transitive graph: the largest pinning and verification burden of all options. Upstreamable: journeys could later become a variant in player-reference-examples . Kotlin 2.3 / AGP 8.11 / JDK 21; its build-logic and code generation ( ig-codegen ) are ours to audit. Much of the template (auth, sync, workforce registers) is unrelated to the journeys and is noise in a demonstrator. Option B — Own lean Compose Multiplatform app on the OHS KMP libraries (recommended) A small Compose Multiplatform app (Android first, web target alongside) written for the four journeys, using the same foundational libraries the Player uses — fhir-model-r4 , fhir-engine (on-device store), fhir-data-capture (SDC questionnaires for J2 registration and J3 import), fhir-workflow ( PlanDefinition/$apply for the J3 schedule) — and, optionally, dev.ohs.player:client for configuration-driven views. Pros Cons --- --- Same current OHS libraries as the Player, so it demonstrates the stack the OHS Foundation is building towards, without the template's auth/sync/DI layer. Not the Player app itself; screens are ours. Offline and serverless from the start; the emulator CI job can drive the journeys. The KMP libraries are alpha: API breaks between alphas are ours to absorb. Dependency set is roughly the libraries' own graph (Compose MP, Ktor client, Room3/SQLite, kotlinx) — still sizeable, but every addition is chosen and listed in docs/dependencies.md . fhir-workflow has no CQL yet: the J3 schedule rules must be expressed as PlanDefinition applicability conditions in FHIRPath (enough for a birth-dose schedule; WHO SMART immunization CQL would wait). Shapes the code so the journey screens can later be offered to player-reference-examples as a Player variant. Option C — Android only, on android-fhir (first generation) A plain Android app on com.google.android.fhir Engine + SDC (+ Workflow). Pros Cons --- --- Mature, production-proven (OpenSRP, EmCare); most documentation and examples. In maintenance; not where OHS is going; Android only (no web). Workflow library runs CQL today (WHO SMART Guidelines content). Workflow pulls HAPI FHIR + CQL engine: a very large, JVM-heavy dependency graph. Google Maven artifacts; the session's network policy currently blocks dl.google.com (needed for this and for AGP/AndroidX in every option). Option D — Web first, no Android app A static page on gh-pages running J1–J4 in the browser with the Rust/wasm library (or a future browser build of hcert-core), plus only the Android test module for STT-GEN-004. Pros Cons --- --- Smallest: almost no dependencies; easiest to show anyone with a link. Not OHS; does not show the Kotlin library inside an OHS app, which is the stated goal. The Rust/wasm library already runs in the browser. The Kotlin library on Android is exercised only by tests, not by a journey. 4. Recommendation Option B , staged: 1. Android test module for STT-GEN-004 first (independent of this choice). 2. The B app, Android target, offline, J1–J4, on dev.ohs.fhir engine + data capture + workflow. 3. The web target of the same app once hcert-core has a browser target (to be requested in smart-trust-tools) — or, in the meantime, the journeys' QR steps on the web through the Rust/wasm library. 4. Later, propose the journeys to the OHS Foundation as a player-reference-examples variant (owner's call; never pushed from here). If being the OHS Player matters more than dependency count and an offline demo, choose A : the plan is the same, with step 2 starting from the template and adding the offline mode first. 5. What any option needs from the environment dl.google.com (Google Maven: AGP, AndroidX, the Android SDK) is blocked by this session's network policy. It is needed to write the Gradle verification metadata for any Android build. GitHub's runners can reach it, so CI is unaffected; local builds here are. Sources OHS Foundation on GitHub — repository list and descriptions, 2026-10-23. ohs-player README, player-reference README, player-client README, kotlin-fhir-engine README, kotlin-fhir-workflow README. Maven Central metadata for dev.ohs.fhir and dev.ohs.player (versions and publication dates). Android FHIR SDK and its Workflow library. WHO joins the Open Health Stack Software Foundation, WHO, July 2026.

User stories Role I want to So that --- --- --- Caregiver Have my daughter's birth doses recognised at home they are not repeated and she stays on schedule Caregiver Show every family member's records abroad from one phone with one passcode each a doctor abroad can treat us without paper or an app Birth clinic vaccinator Print a signed record of each birth dose the family can carry anywhere Community health worker Read a foreign vaccination QR offline and register the child with it the clinic sees what was given before the family arrives Community health worker Refer a child whose foreign record needs checking verification is done by someone who can Home clinic provider Know whether a foreign certificate is genuine, and why not when it is not Home clinic provider See which doses are due once the foreign doses are imported I give only what is missing Point-of-care provider Read a visiting child's summary and vaccinations from a QR the parent shows without installing anything or calling another country User scenarios Each step names the requirements of smart-trust-tools it exercises. The stories are in scenarios/stories.json . J1 — Cross-border birth and initial vaccination (Country A) Precondition: the issuer's DSC is on the trust list. XXR's document signer certificate (DSC), issued under XXR's Country Signing CA (CSCA), was shared with the GDHCN, the Trust Anchor, before any DVC is signed; the GDHCN publishes it as a DID document. Sharing it is not a step of issuing. A DVC signed with a key whose DSC was never shared fails every receiver's trust-list check (STT-VER-006). Mali gives birth to Chanthala on 2026-10-21 at a provincial hospital in Country A, while visiting relatives. Dr Pimchanok WATTANA gives the Hep B and BCG birth doses and records them. For each dose, the hospital system does three things: 1. It builds a DVCMinPreQual payload: STT-PAY-001…005 and STT-PAY-007, with subclaim −6 (STT-SEL-003). 2. It prepares the CWT and the bytes to sign: STT-CWT-001…005, STT-ISS-004. 3. It has XXR's key sign them (STT-COS-002, STT-COS-006), then finishes the HC1 text: STT-COS-001, STT-ZIP-001, STT-B45-001, STT-HC1-001, STT-QR-001. Mali leaves with two paper DVCs. In the demo: the guide's two signed HC1 strings stand in for the hospital's output. Live issuance in the app uses a TEST-ONLY key (STT-ISS-003), whose DSC is not on the GDHCN list, so its DVCs do not verify in J3. J2 — Return home, CHW discovery and referral (Country B) Back in Country B, Sita RAI finds Chanthala missing from the household register on a home visit. Sita has no signal. She scans both QRs. The CHW app reads them with read-unverified (STT-VER-011; STT-B45-002, STT-ZIP-002, STT-CBR-003), which needs no trust list. It shows the doses, marked unverified. Sita registers Chanthala and refers her to the clinic. Everything syncs that evening. J3 — Clinic verification and schedule generation (Country B) Precondition: the DID documents are already loaded. Loading them is not a step of this visit. The clinic may be offline all day, so the EHR fetches nothing during it: its trust store holds the GDHCN DEV trust list as it was last refreshed, including XXR's DSC DID document (STT-TRU-001, STT-TRU-002, STT-TRU-005). A clinic with no connection of its own refreshes it about weekly, when the CHW visits the base clinic or district health office, where Country B retrieves the list the GDHCN trust anchor distributes. A DSC published after that refresh is not in the clinic's copy, so its DVC fails the trust-list check (STT-VER-006) until the next refresh. Tomas ALVES opens the referral and scans the QRs. The EHR verifies each DVC offline against that copy (STT-VER-001…009, STT-KID-002). Both verify, so it imports them as FHIR Immunization s with provenance (STT-VER-007, STT-VER-008). The national schedule then runs: the birth doses count, and birth-dose OPV is due. Tomas gives it. If a DVC fails, the EHR names the step and the reason, and Tomas decides by national policy. J4.0 — "One Family, One Phone" (Country B) Precondition, as in J1: Country B's DSC, under Country B's CSCA, is already shared with the GDHCN, the Trust Anchor. That is what lets the hospital abroad verify the link in J4.1. The family plans a trip. On the national portal, Mali asks for each member's records. For each member, the portal does three things: 1. It assembles an IPS and that member's DVCs. 2. It encrypts them (STT-VHL-004, STT-VHL-007) behind a passcode-protected manifest with an expiry (STT-VHL-009). 3. It issues the link as an HCERT, with the VHL at key 5 (STT-VHL-001, STT-VHL-002), signed with Country B's DSC. The shared phone holds one QR per member. J4.1 — Point of care abroad Precondition, as in J3: the DID documents are already loaded. The hospital system's trust store is a cached copy of the GDHCN trust list, including Country B's DSC DID document (STT-TRU-001, STT-TRU-002, STT-TRU-005). The hospital refreshes it nightly or hourly, against about weekly at the offline J3 clinic. It does not need to be online to verify: verifying reads the cache and never fetches the list. A DSC published after the last refresh fails the trust-list check (STT-VER-006), naming that reason. Abroad, Chanthala has a fever. Mali shows Chanthala's QR on the family phone and tells Dr Ana MOREIRA the passcode. The hospital system takes four steps: 1. It verifies the HCERT against Country B's DSC in that copy of the trust list. 2. It requests the manifest by ITI-YY5, signed with HTTP Message Signatures (STT-VHL-005, STT-VHL-006, STT-VHL-008). 3. It decrypts the IPS and DVCs (STT-VHL-007). 4. It shows them to Dr Ana MOREIRA. If the HCERT does not verify (for example, Country B's DSC is missing from the cached list), there is no digital verification. The hospital names the step and the reason (STT-VER-008), does not follow the VHL, and Dr Ana MOREIRA treats whatever the family can show as she would a paper record.

Filed as smart-trust-phw 18; fix offered as smart-trust-phw 19. Title: Requirement receive-a-vhl names the Issuer as its actor; it should be the Receiver In input/fsh/requirements/requirements.fsh , the Requirements instance receive-a-vhl ("Receive VHL or VDHC") reads: description = "Is able to receive a VHL authorization mechanism or a VDHC from a Holder" actor[+] = Canonical(Issuer) The capability described, receiving a VHL or VDHC from a Holder, is the Receiver 's ( ActorDefinition/Receiver : "Receiver (system) of Verifiable Health Certificate or Verifiable Health Link"). Its counterpart provide-a-vhl-to-a-receiver names the Holder. Proposed fix: diff actor[+] = Canonical(Issuer) actor[+] = Canonical(Receiver) The same change is applied in litlfred/smart-trust-phw (https://github.com/litlfred/smart-trust-phw/pull/1) and can be offered as a pull request here. Found while mapping the user journeys of litlfred/smart-trust-demo (a CHW app, a clinic EHR and a hospital system abroad each receive a VDHC or VHL from the Holder) to the guide's actors.
